subject: chemistry
title: Properties and combustion of hydrocarbons
key_idea: As hydrocarbon molecules get larger, boiling point and viscosity increase and flammability decreases. Hydrocarbon fuels burn in complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.

blocks.text: Three properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules. These properties decide how each hydrocarbon is used as a fuel.

items.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid turns to a gas.
How difficult it is for a liquid to flow. A thick liquid has high viscosity.
How easily a substance catches fire and burns.

items: As the number of carbon atoms increases, the **boiling point** increases.

blocks.text: The boiling point rises because the weak forces between larger molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to separate them.

diagram.alt: Small hydrocarbon molecules compared with large hydrocarbon molecules.

items: In an investigation, a more viscous liquid takes longer to flow through a funnel.
Small molecules make good fuels because they ignite easily and flow easily.
Larger molecules have higher boiling points and are more viscous.
The boiling point trend is explained by stronger forces between larger molecules.

blocks.text: Hydrocarbon fuels burn in oxygen and release energy. In complete combustion, the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised.

items.meaning: Burning a substance in oxygen, which releases energy.
Combined with oxygen. The carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water.

blocks.label: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon
where: energy is released (the reaction is exothermic)

items: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces **carbon dioxide** and **water**.
The water forms as water vapour, which condenses on a cold surface.

blocks.text: Balance the equation so there are the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

items.text: Balance the carbon atoms with the number of CO₂.
Balance the hydrogen atoms with the number of H₂O.
Count the oxygen atoms on the right and balance them with O₂.

diagram.question: Two molecules of an alkane with **{n}** carbon atoms burn completely: 2CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + ___ O₂ → ___ CO₂ + ___ H₂O. How many O₂ molecules are needed?

items: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water and releases energy.
Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen.

checks.q: Explain the trend in the boiling points of the alkanes C₅H₁₂ (36 °C), C₁₀H₂₂ (174 °C) and C₁₅H₃₂ (271 °C).
checks.a: The boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases. The forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces) increase as the size of the molecules increases.

checks.q: Heavy fuel oil is more viscous than kerosene. Justify this.
checks.a: Viscosity increases as molecular size increases, and heavy fuel oil has larger molecules than kerosene.

checks.q: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of propane: C₃H₈ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O

exam_phrases: the boiling point increases as the number of (carbon) atoms increases
as molecular size increases viscosity increases
heavy fuel oil has larger molecules (than kerosene)

mistakes.wrong: The boiling point increases because the covalent bonds between the atoms get stronger.
mistakes.right: An incorrect reference to particles or bonds limits the answer to 2 marks. Say the weak forces between the molecules increase as the molecules get larger.

mistakes.wrong: The forces between molecules increase, so the boiling point increases.
mistakes.right: The second mark depends on the first. State the trend first: the boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases.
An unbalanced equation with no multipliers earns 1 mark. Balance it: C₉H₂₀ + 14O₂ → 9CO₂ + 10H₂O.

worked_example.question:
This question is about crude oil and alkanes.

The boiling points of three alkanes are: C₅H₁₂ 36 °C, C₁₀H₂₂ 174 °C and C₁₅H₃₂ 271 °C.

Explain the trend in the boiling points of the alkanes.
answer_points: The boiling point increases as the number of (carbon) atoms increases.
Because the (weak) intermolecular forces, the forces between the molecules, increase.
These forces increase as the size of the molecules increases.
worked_example.tip: The second mark depends on the first. Referring to particles or bonds instead of forces between molecules limits the answer to 2 marks.

mistakes.wrong: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + hydrogen
mistakes.right: Other substances on either side lose the mark. The products are carbon dioxide and water only.

mistakes.wrong: C₈H₁₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O with different numbers of atoms on each side.
mistakes.right: Marks are given separately for the left formulae, the right formulae and the balancing. A balanced equation needs correct formulae first: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O.

worked_example.question: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈.
answer_points: Balanced: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O (any correct multiple, including halves, is allowed).
worked_example.tip: State symbols are ignored. One mark each for the reactants, the products and the balancing.

blocks.text: Alkenes also burn completely in oxygen. The hydrocarbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.

exam_phrases: as the number of carbon atoms increases the boiling point increases
larger molecules have greater intermolecular forces
the stronger the intermolecular forces the higher the boiling point

mistakes.right: The words and and & are not allowed in place of +. Write C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O.

mistakes.wrong: The boiling point is higher because the covalent bonds in larger molecules are stronger.
mistakes.right: References to covalent bonds are not allowed. Say the intermolecular forces between larger molecules are stronger.
The balancing mark depends on correct formulae, although 1 mark can be given for a balanced equation with a minor error in case or subscripts.

worked_example.question:
Look at the data about some hydrocarbons.

ethane: 2 carbon atoms, C₂H₆, boiling point −88 °C
propane: 3 carbon atoms, C₃H₈, boiling point −42 °C
pentane: 5 carbon atoms, C₅H₁₂, boiling point 36 °C
hexane: 6 carbon atoms, C₆H₁₄, boiling point 69 °C

Describe the relationship between the number of carbon atoms in the molecule and its boiling point.
Use ideas about forces between molecules to explain your answer.
answer_points: As the number of carbon atoms increases, the boiling point increases.
Larger molecules have greater intermolecular forces.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the trend and one for the explanation in terms of forces between molecules.
